html:
Introduction

Starting a Nursing Facility in Tennessee represents a meaningful opportunity to serve seniors and adults requiring 24-hour skilled nursing care, post-acute rehabilitation, or long-term medical supervision while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the Tennessee Health Facilities Commission (THFC), which is the primary state licensing body. Reimbursement and program funding for a significant portion of residents are coordinated through Tennessee’s Medicaid program, TennCare CHOICES. This structure creates a clear, albeit complex, regulatory and financial pathway for new providers.

With a mature and competitive market of approximately 300 existing providers and TennCare reimbursement rates in the $180-$250 per day range, Tennessee offers a competitive but opportunity-rich environment for providers prepared to navigate its rigorous licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. Success often hinges on identifying a specific niche, such as post-acute rehabilitation, specialized memory care, or high-acuity ventilator care, and achieving a high CMS star rating to attract referrals.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Nursing Facility in Tennessee, from understanding the critical Certificate of Need (CON) process and state regulations to staffing your facility, managing reimbursement, and preparing for state and federal inspections.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Tennessee’s Nursing Facility Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Tennessee’s Nursing Facility Regulations

Tennessee regulates Nursing Facilities through the Tennessee Health Facilities Commission (THFC). This agency is responsible for issuing Certificates of Need (CONs), initial licensure, renewals, and conducting compliance oversight for nursing homes. The CON process is a critical first step, requiring you to prove a public need for new nursing home beds in your proposed service area. This is a significant barrier to entry and requires a detailed, data-driven application.

Providers serving Medicaid or Medicare populations, which constitute the vast majority of nursing facilities, must also comply with federal frameworks established by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). These federal regulations, known as the Requirements of Participation, are extensive and govern nearly every aspect of facility operations. Compliance with HIPAA for patient privacy and OSHA for workplace safety is also mandatory.

The state and federal regulatory framework emphasizes resident safety, quality of care, infection control, and resident rights. This includes detailed rules on care planning, medication management, staffing levels, and maintaining a safe, homelike environment. Licenses in Tennessee typically require renewal every 1 to 2 years, contingent on successful completion of annual surveys and maintaining good standing.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

While all licensed facilities provide skilled nursing, Tennessee supports multiple specialized service niches, each with different staffing, equipment, and reimbursement considerations. Differentiating your facility is key to success in a competitive market.

  • Skilled Nursing & Post-Acute Rehabilitation: This model focuses on short-term stays for patients recovering from surgery, cardiac events, or significant illness. It requires strong relationships with local hospitals and a robust therapy department (Physical, Occupational, and Speech Therapy).
  • Long-Term Custodial Care: This traditional model provides ongoing medical and personal care for residents with chronic conditions who can no longer live independently. It relies heavily on TennCare and private pay funding.
  • Specialized Memory Care Units: These are secure, specially designed units for individuals with Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia. They require staff with specialized training in dementia care and programming tailored to cognitive impairment.
  • High-Acuity Care (Ventilator/Tracheostomy): A highly specialized niche, these units care for residents requiring mechanical ventilation or tracheostomy care. This model commands higher reimbursement rates but requires significant investment in equipment and staff with critical care skills.

Program size in Tennessee typically ranges from 50 to 200+ beds. Demand for services is strongest in metropolitan areas like Nashville, Memphis, Knoxville, and Chattanooga, where large hospital systems create strong referral pipelines for post-acute care. Conversely, rural counties may have fewer providers and less competition for long-term care beds, but these areas may also offer challenges related to workforce availability and a smaller private pay population.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can apply for a license, you must establish a formal business entity. Providers typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or Corporation (S-Corp or C-Corp) to protect personal assets from business liabilities. Your legal and financial advisors can help you choose the best structure for your goals.

To formalize your business and begin the licensing process, you must:

  • Register your business with the Tennessee Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS for tax purposes.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (malpractice), and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a Certificate of Need (CON) application to the THFC, which is the most challenging and lengthy part of the process.
  • Upon CON approval, submit a licensing application to the THFC, which includes architectural plans, proof of financial viability, and operational policies.

Licensing timelines in Tennessee are extensive, generally ranging from 12 to 24 months or longer. This extended timeframe is primarily due to the competitive and data-intensive Certificate of Need (CON) process, which can involve legal challenges and multiple review cycles.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A detailed business plan is essential for securing financing and guiding your operational strategy. Startup costs for a nursing facility in Tennessee are substantial, typically ranging from $3 million to $15 million+, depending on whether you build a new facility or acquire and renovate an existing one, as well as the total bed count.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by labor, with staffing representing 55% to 65% of total costs. Other major expenses include mortgage/lease, utilities, raw food, medical supplies, insurance, and maintenance. Your financial projections must be grounded in a realistic payor mix.

Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in Tennessee include:

  • TennCare CHOICES (Medicaid): $180 – $250 per patient day, forming the financial backbone for most long-term care residents.
  • Medicare Part A (Post-Acute): Significantly higher rates, often ranging from $400 – $600+ per day for the first 20 days of a qualifying post-hospital stay.
  • Private Pay: Can range from $250 – $400+ per day, depending on location, amenities, and room type (private vs. semi-private).

With a strong focus on expense management and maintaining a high census, providers operating at a target occupancy of 85-90% can generally achieve 3-8% profit margins. Reaching break-even often takes 18-24 months post-opening.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility

Your physical facility must meet stringent state and federal standards to ensure resident safety and well-being. Whether building new or renovating, the building must comply with the Life Safety Code, Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), and specific state licensing rules.

Key facility requirements include:

  • ADA-compliant rooms, bathrooms, and common areas.
  • A nurse call system accessible from each resident’s bed and bathroom.
  • A full commercial kitchen capable of meeting the dietary needs of all residents.
  • Specific square footage per resident room and limitations on the number of residents per room.
  • Dedicated dining rooms and activity spaces.
  • Fire suppression systems, including sprinklers and a monitored fire alarm.
  • Secure entries and exits, especially for facilities with memory care units.

Location selection is a strategic decision. You should consider local zoning regulations, proximity to hospitals and physician offices for referrals, accessibility for families, and the availability of a qualified healthcare workforce.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Staffing is the single most important factor in delivering quality care and maintaining compliance. Tennessee and CMS regulations mandate specific roles and staffing levels. You must have a plan to recruit, train, and retain a dedicated team.

Required roles in a nursing facility typically include:

  • Licensed Nursing Home Administrator (LNHA): The overall manager of the facility, who must hold a current Tennessee LNHA license.
  • Director of Nursing (DON): A Registered Nurse (RN) responsible for overseeing all clinical care and nursing staff.
  • Registered Nurses (RNs): Provide skilled assessments, treatments, and supervision.
  • Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs): Administer medications and provide direct nursing care under the supervision of an RN.
  • Certified Nursing Assistants (CNAs): Provide the majority of direct personal care and assistance with daily living.
  • MDS Coordinator: An RN responsible for completing the Minimum Data Set assessments that determine Medicare/Medicaid reimbursement levels.
  • Social Services Director
  • Activities Director
  • Dietary Manager

All staff must undergo comprehensive training upon hire and annually thereafter. Training requirements include state-specific administrator licensure, professional licensure for nurses, CNA certification, dementia care training (for staff in memory care units), infection control, resident rights, abuse prevention, and HIPAA. All licensed staff must also complete ongoing continuing education units (CEUs) to maintain their credentials.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Your facility cannot operate without a comprehensive set of written policies and procedures. These documents are the backbone of your operation, guiding staff actions and demonstrating compliance to surveyors. Tennessee requires written policies covering all aspects of care and administration.

Key policy areas include:

  • Resident Rights: Protecting the dignity, choice, and privacy of every resident.
  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge: Criteria and processes for resident movement.
  • Infection Prevention and Control: Protocols for hand hygiene, PPE, outbreak management, and reporting.
  • Emergency Preparedness: A detailed plan for natural disasters, fires, or other emergencies.
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI): A data-driven program to continuously monitor and improve care.
  • Medication Management: Procedures for ordering, storing, administering, and destroying medications.
  • Staffing and Training: Plans for ensuring adequate staffing levels and ongoing staff competency.
  • Abuse, Neglect, and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting.

In addition to facility-wide policies, individual care plans must be developed for each resident. These person-centered plans are based on comprehensive assessments and outline the resident’s specific needs, goals, and preferences. They must be developed by an interdisciplinary team, reviewed regularly, and documented meticulously per Tennessee and federal rules.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Unlike many consumer-facing businesses, marketing a nursing facility is less about public advertising and more about building professional relationships. Your primary customers are not the residents themselves, but the healthcare professionals who refer them.

Referrals for nursing facilities in Tennessee typically come from:

  • Hospital discharge planners and case managers: This is the most critical referral source, especially for lucrative short-term rehabilitation stays.
  • Physicians and specialty medical practices.
  • Home health agencies and hospice providers.
  • Managed care organizations (MCOs) and insurance case managers.
  • Tennessee’s Area Agency on Aging and Disability (AAAD) offices.

Successful providers focus on demonstrating compliance, clinical excellence, responsiveness, and superior outcomes. Your facility’s CMS Star Rating, which is publicly available on the Medicare Care Compare website, is your most powerful marketing tool. A high star rating signals quality and safety to both referral sources and families, making it a top operational priority.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Oversight of your nursing facility is continuous and rigorous. Your facility will be subject to unannounced inspections (surveys) from surveying bodies including the Tennessee Health Facilities Commission (THFC) and, by extension, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

These inspections are comprehensive, focusing on direct observation of care, resident and staff interviews, and a thorough review of documentation. Surveyors are trained to identify systemic problems, and deficiencies can result in fines, a directed plan of correction, or even loss of licensure.

Common deficiencies cited in nursing home surveys often relate to:

  • Infection control lapses (e.g., improper hand hygiene, PPE usage).
  • Medication administration errors.
  • Failure to prevent or properly treat pressure ulcers.
  • Violations of resident rights.
  • Incomplete or inaccurate care planning and documentation.

To succeed, you must foster a culture of continuous quality improvement (CQI) and maintain audit-ready documentation at all times. A robust QAPI program is not just a regulatory requirement; it is the essential framework for identifying and correcting issues before they become survey deficiencies.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

  • How long does it take to open a Nursing Facility in Tennessee?

The entire process, from planning to opening, can take 18 to 36 months. The Certificate of Need (CON) application and approval process is the most time-consuming phase and can significantly impact your timeline.

  • What licenses are required?

You need a Certificate of Need (CON) and a Nursing Home license from the Tennessee Health Facilities Commission (THFC). Additionally, the facility must be certified by CMS to accept Medicare and enrolled as a provider with TennCare to accept Medicaid.

  • What reimbursement is available?

Reimbursement comes from three primary sources: TennCare (Medicaid) at rates of approximately $180-$250/day for long-term care, Medicare for short-term post-acute care (at much higher daily rates), and private pay from residents and their families.

Conclusion

Starting a Nursing Facility in Tennessee is a complex and capital-intensive endeavor that requires careful planning, deep regulatory understanding, and unwavering operational discipline. The path to licensure is long, marked by the critical Certificate of Need process. However, for entrepreneurs who are committed to excellence, the opportunity to serve a vulnerable population and build a lasting business is significant. Providers who invest in a strong clinical team, a culture of compliance, and strategic referral relationships are best positioned for long-term success in Tennessee’s established healthcare landscape.
